title: Nike x One Piece collection brings Devil Fruits to sneakers and streetwear in Japan
description: One Piece sets sail for global domination with a Nike collection inspired by the manga and anime’s superpowers. One Piece fans will soon be able to slip into some awesome powers from the world of manga and anime, thanks to a new collection from Nike inspired by Devil Fruits. The new Nike x One Piece […]
content:
One Piece sets sail for global domination with a Nike collection inspired by the manga and anime’s superpowers.

One Piece fans will soon be able to slip into some awesome powers from the world of manga and anime, thanks to a new collection from Nike inspired by Devil Fruits.

The new Nike x One Piece collection includes three special-edition Air Max Plus designs, along with jerseys, T-shirts, caps and a vest, with details that conjure up the supernatural powers received by consuming a Devil Fruit. While the collection will eventually be available globally, the first port of call is Japan, where customers will have the chance to get their hands on the collection ahead of other countries, at a special three-day pop-up in Tokyo beginning on 4 September.

The journey starts with Devil Fruit swirls on the kicks, which are priced at 27,500 yen (US$173.10) in Japan, or US$210 in the U.S. as the global standard pricing.

▼ Nike Air Max Plus SP “Gomu Gomu”

This purple-and-green pair takes its inspiration from Gomu Gomu no Mi, the Devil Fruit associated with Monkey D. Luffy, which gives him rubber-like abilities.

Whisper “Gomu Gomu no…” while wearing these and you’ll instantly feel like you can call upon rubbery superpowers to get you out of any sticky scenarios.

▼ Nike Air Max Plus SP “Ope Ope”

Berry-red and green hues conjure up the powers of Ope Ope no Mi, the Devil Fruit that takes you to a “Room” where you can manipulate objects and people at will.

While these sneakers won’t actually grant you eternal youth, they’ll make you look and feel young every time you wear them.

▼ Nike Air Max Plus SP “Mera Mera” 

The fiery orange, yellow and green colour scheme of the Mera Mera no Mi makes its presence felt on this bright pair of kicks, which will help to keep everyone out of your way whenever you step out in them.

The shoes are complemented by matching Air Max Plus jerseys and caps drawn from the Nike archive, which will be released alongside a range of exclusive apparel, so you can express your love for One Piece above the knee.

▼ Nike Solo Swoosh T-Shirt QS “Promise of Battle” (6,930 yen)

This eyecatching design, available in black and white colourways, features the pirate flag drawn by Monkey D. Luffy, with a large red Swoosh giving it a Nike twist.

▼ Nike Solo Swoosh T-Shirt QS “Gomu Gomu no Ono” (9,680 yen)

Luffy’s “Gomu Gomu no Ono” (“Gum-Gum Battle Axe”) gets the full manga treatment on this T-shirt, with a dramatic panel showing the stretchy pirate captain unleashing the powerful move across the back.

In addition to a couple of other yet-to-be-released T-shirt designs, there’s also an exclusive Nike Vest (45,100 yen).


The vest may be pretty hard to get in Japan, as it’s listed as a Tokyo pop-up exclusive and will be available at Dr. B’s Research Lab, a three-day-only pop-up store in Tokyo’s Harajuku district from 4 to 6 September. The pop-up will stock the collection as well as a special T-shirt exclusive to the event, but entry to the venue and purchases of eligible products will be limited to people who win the advance lottery (details at the bottom of this page), which is open for applications from 7:30 p.m. on 23 August until 11:59 p.m. on 26 August.

Fans in Japan who want to put their own spin on the collaboration can also head to the Nike By You customisation service at Nike Harajuku and Nike Umeda, where nine custom graphics will be available.

▼ Small graphics are 1,000 yen each, while large sizes are 1,200 yen.

The customisation experience will be available at Nike Harajuku from 4 to 11 September, with reservations accepted from 10 a.m.–9 p.m. on each day during this period, followed by Nike Umeda from 12 to 19 September, where reservations will be accepted from 11 a.m.–9 p.m. Reservations will be taken on a first-come, first-served basis until capacity is reached.

▼ Celebrate your own personal connection to One Piece by mixing and matching the graphics to create a one-of-a-kind T-shirt that’s unique to you.

As the first port of call for the collection, it’s a very good time to be a One Piece fan in Japan. Following the pop-up store event, the Mera Mera range will be sold at Nike Umeda in Osaka on 12 September, ahead of the collection’s global release through Nike’s SNKRS app on 25 September. Other countries around the world will also have their own pop-up events from 12 September onwards, so check the SNKRS app for more details.

title: Winnie the Pooh cosplays as Yuzuru Hanyu for new plushie collaboration
description: Apparently it’s not a bother at all for Pooh Bear to dress up like the Japanese skating star. Yuzuru Hanyu’s fondness for Winnie the Pooh is well known, and the Japanese figure skating legend’s fanbase has created a tradition of showering the ice with plushies of the character after his performances. But is Pooh Bear […]
content:
Apparently it’s not a bother at all for Pooh Bear to dress up like the Japanese skating star.

Yuzuru Hanyu’s fondness for Winnie the Pooh is well known, and the Japanese figure skating legend’s fanbase has created a tradition of showering the ice with plushies of the character after his performances. But is Pooh Bear himself one of Hanyu’s fans?

That might seem like an impossible question to answer, given that Winnie the Pooh, like most fictional animated characters, isn’t in the habit of giving interviews. But as they say, actions speak louder than words, and so it’s probably safe to say that Pooh likes Hanyu too, since he’s now cosplaying as the skater.

Publisher Kodansha is getting set to release To Pooh-san: Yuzuru Hanyu and Pooh-san Memory Book. The 40-page book contains a photo collection and exclusive interview with Hanyu, and to sweeten the deal, it comes bundled with a 20.5-centimeter (8.1-inch) tall Winnie the Pooh plushie. For this collaboration, Pooh is forgoing his customary red polo shirt and instead going with more fantastic fashions.

The plushie comes with two outfits, recreating the costumes worn by Hanyu at the 2018 Pyeongchang Winter Olympics, where he won the second of his gold medals. The ensemble Pooh is wearing in the above image is the same as the one Hanyu wore for his free-skate program to the musical piece titled “Seimei.”

And if you change Pooh into his alternate included set of clothes, he’ll match what Hanyu was wearing for his short program skate to Chopin’s “Ballade No. 1.”

Also part of the package are a 51.5 x 72.8-centimeter poster and reproduction of a handwritten note that Yuzuru penned to Pooh.

Kodansha is asking 22,000 yen (US$138) for To Pooh-san: Yuzuru Hanyu and Pooh-san Memory Book and its bundled merch, and all units are being produced to order. On the one hand, that means that pre-ordering is required, but it also means that actual fans are guaranteed to be able to purchase the set without having to go through a scalper.

▼ Yuzuru posing with Pooh dressing as Yuzuru…honestly, this does seem like a missed opportunity for the skater to have worn the bear’s shirt.

Pre-orders are open between now and October 20 through Amazon Japan and Rakuten (here and here), with Amazon listing shipping as slated for late May of 2027. And if you need even more Yuzuru Hanyu/Winnie the Pooh crossover merch, there’s the pair’s also recently revealed Shower of Heart collection.

title: Nagoya’s famous Shinkansen platform noodle shop has other, better branches nearby
description: Travelers love Sumiyoshi’s kishimen, but there’s a way to skip the long line and get a better deal on your meal. Nagoya an outstanding destination for traveling foodies, thanks to the city’s numerous tasty claims to fame, including tempura shrimp rice balls, a special kind of local miso, and a unique breakfast culture. Then there’s […]
content:
Travelers love Sumiyoshi’s kishimen, but there’s a way to skip the long line and get a better deal on your meal.

Nagoya an outstanding destination for traveling foodies, thanks to the city’s numerous tasty claims to fame, including tempura shrimp rice balls, a special kind of local miso, and a unique breakfast culture. Then there’s Nagoya’s representative type of noodles, kishimen, broad udon noodles with a soy sauce-based broth.

Kishimen is so strongly associated with Nagoya that you can even find great places to try it inside Nagoya Station. Travelers regularly form a long line outside Sumiyoshi, a stand-and-eat kishimen joint on the Shinkansen platform.

▼ The Shinkansen platform Sumiyoshi

However, while passing through Nagoya Station the other day we found out that Sumiyoshi also has kishimen stands on three non-Shinkansen platforms, and these are the better ones to go to, for two reasons. First, they’re less crowded, or at least they were when we stopped by on a weekday afternoon. At that time, the Shinkansen platform branch, as usual, had a line to get in, but we could walk right into the Sumiyoshi on the non-Shinkansen Line 5/6 platform Sumiyoshi with no waiting.

▼ The Line 5/6 platform Sumiyoshi

The other reason to visit one of the non-Shinkansen Sumiyoshi branches? The One-coin Kishimen, which is exclusive to the regular-line branches.

▼ ワンコインきしめん = One-coin Kishimen

The “one coin” here refers to the price of just 500 yen (US$3.15), which is also the largest-denomination yen coin. Suiyoshi already charges 450 yen for a bowl of just plain kishimen noodles, and most topping options beyond some simple seaweed will cost you 700 yen or more. The One-coin Kishimen, though, is a thoroughly satisfying bargain.

Along with the noodles, you get a nicely sized tempura shrimp, some aburaage (fried tofu), katsuobushi (bonito flakes) and sliced green onion.

This isn’t a mini portion of kishimen to make up for the toppings, either. It’s a full-sized serving of noodles, with barely any additional charge for all the extras that are in the bowl with them. And the low price isn’t the result of the non-Shinkansen Sumiyoshi branches using lower-quality ingredients or skimping on seasonings either. We asked the staff if there was any difference between how the regular and Shinkansen-line locations prepare their noodles, and were informed that they all make their kishimen the exact same way.

All it took was a single taste to confirm that the staff was telling the truth. This tasted every bit as good as the Sumiyoshi kishimen we’d eaten on the Shinkansen platform on a previous visit, just at a more budget-friendly price.

In addition to the Line 5/6 platform branch that we ate at, Sumiyoshi also has kishimen stands on the Line 1/2 and 3/4 platforms, and it’s a pretty safe bet that their noodles are equally delicious. And should you be looking for dessert afterwards, Krispy Kreme Japan has some special donuts in Nagoya that you can’t get anywhere else in the world.

title: Osaka Starbucks has one of the city’s coolest photo vantage points, but it’s going away soon
description: We head to Osaka to say goodbye to Ebitsuta, and get a new view at one of the city’s most famous landmarks. The physical media market definitely isn’t what it used to be. Back when he was a college student in Osaka, our Japanese-language reporter Seiji Nakazawa spent countless hours hanging out in the Ebisubashi […]
content:
We head to Osaka to say goodbye to Ebitsuta, and get a new view at one of the city’s most famous landmarks.

The physical media market definitely isn’t what it used to be. Back when he was a college student in Osaka, our Japanese-language reporter Seiji Nakazawa spent countless hours hanging out in the Ebisubashi branch of multimedia chain Tsutaya. Located in the Dotonbori entertainment district, Ebitsuta, as the cool kids called this Tsutaya, had just recently opened, and was stocked with so many CDs and movies to rent or buy that it felt like an enchanted forest of audio/video wonders. As an aspiring rock guitarist, Seiji regularly got blissfully lost looking through the gigantic music selection, and if he was meeting up with friends in the neighborhood, he’d often get there early and tell them to come find him at Ebitsuta.

Sadly, though, Ebitsuta’s days are numbered. With fewer and fewer people buying or renting physical media, Tsutaya has spent the last several years dramatically restructuring, and now the decision has been made to close the Ebisubashi branch, which opened all the way back in 2003. Thankfully, Ebitsuta will still be open for a few more months, which meant Seiji had time to go back recently and say goodbye, and also to find a great photo-snapping vantage point.

Since he moved to Tokyo not long after graduating, it’s actually been a very long time since Seiji stopped by this Tsutaya, and stepping inside, he found out that in many ways it’s already pivoted away from its former foci. The basement floor, for example, now houses the Osaka IP Shoten, Tsutaya’s sub-brand for anime character merch.

There is still a music vibe going on, though, thanks to how huge a presence virtual YouTubers, many of which have vocalist side hustles, now have in the otaku sphere. This Ebitsuta Osaka IP Shoten seems to be especially oriented towards female fans, with huge standees of male VTuber group Eden-gumi waiting at the entrance to greet shoppers when Seiji visited, and a comparatively smaller section for female performers.

Next, let’s skip ahead to the third floor, which is devoted to…

…cosmetics? At first, Seiji thought this might be a non-Tsutaya tenant who was renting out the third floor, but actually this is another example of the company’s evolving diversification, as it now has its own cosmetic retailing sub-brand, called @Cosme Store/Tsutaya.

Moving up to the four floor, Seiji found it pretty much entirely stocked with idol singer CDs, photo albums, magazines, and other related merchandise. It felt sort of like the flesh-and-blood counterpart to the basement level’s anime goods.

The fifth floor is an event hall, but with nothing on the schedule this day, it was closed to the public. So now let’s head back down to the first floor, where there’s a Starbucks.

In and of itself, that’s nothing to get all that excited about, since there are tons of Starbucks branches in Japan. Still, being in Dotonbori, this is a convenient enough location, and things really get good when you head up to the second floor, where there’s additional seating…

…and a fantastic view of Osaka’s world-famous mechanized crab sign!

The storefront of the main branch of crab specialty restaurant Kani Doraku is a must-see when visiting Osaka, and this might be one of the best places to see it from. When viewed from the street outside, you’re mainly only able to see the bottom half of the creature, and it’s not really visible from inside Kani Doraku itself. The Ebitsuta Starbucks’ second-floor windows, though, let you look at it straight on, allowing you to fully grasp its scale and how intricate its movements are.

▼ You can even see how its eyes move!

The last day for Ebisubashi Tsutaya will be January 11. It’s not clear what’ll happen after that, such as whether the building will be torn down for a replacement or whether new tenants will be moving in to a redistributed and renovated interior. That means that there’s no guarantee that you’ll be able to see this view of Osaka’s mecha crab landmark, so if you’re looking for a place to sip on one of those new Japanese grape Frappuccinos, we’d highly recommend this one.

Location information
Tsutaya Ebisubashi / ツタヤ戎橋
Address: Osaka-fu, Osaka-shi, Chuo-ku, Dotonbori 1-8-19
大阪府大阪市中央区道頓堀１丁目８−１９
Starbucks open 8 a.m.-10:30 p.m.

title: We recommend not buying one pack of Japan’s new convenience store corn soup-flavor fried chicken
description: But that doesn’t mean we don’t love it. Japanese convenience store chain Lawson’s Karaage-kun is one of the absolute all-stars of the combini food world. These bite-sized pieces of karaage (Japanese-style fried chicken), which even come with a toothpick so you can eat them without getting your fingers dirty, are so deliciously satisfying that it’s […]
content:
But that doesn’t mean we don’t love it.

Japanese convenience store chain Lawson’s Karaage-kun is one of the absolute all-stars of the combini food world. These bite-sized pieces of karaage (Japanese-style fried chicken), which even come with a toothpick so you can eat them without getting your fingers dirty, are so deliciously satisfying that it’s hard for us to recall a time when we regretted buying a pack of them.

But while Karaage-kun is a reliable favorite, Lawson still likes to change things up by offering seasonal and limited-time flavors alongside the always-available regular-version Karaage-kun. That’s what brought us to Lawson on a recent afternoon to try their new corn soup-flavored fried chicken.

It might not be a standard-bearer for Japanese cuisine with such global fame as sushi or ramen, but corn soup definitely has a place in the country’s heart and stomach. Anyone who’s traveled in Japan during the fall or winter has probably spotted cans of heated corn soup for sale in vending machines, but you can find it year-round at restaurants that serve Western-style fare in Japan, including steak restaurant chain Asakuma, whose take on corn soup is so popular that it’s sold on its own too.

▼ Asakuma corn soup

You can find Asakuma branches in the Tokyo area, but the chain got its start in Nagoya, and so the Asakuma Corn Soup Karaage-kun is not only a limited-time flavor, but a region-specific one too, only available at Lawson locations in the Tokai and Hokuriku areas that sit between Japan’s eastern Kanto and central Kansai. We were willing to track it down, though, to see how it tastes.

▼ The box’s graphics sport the Asakuma (あさくま) logo.

Japanese-style corn soup, also sometimes called corn potage, is similar to corn chowder, but simpler, creamier, and slightly sweeter. It’s an accessible, widely loved flavor, but would it work well with fried chicken?

As soon as we opened the flap, the inviting aroma of corn soup wafter up out of the box. After spearing a piece of chicken, we popped it into our mouth, and just as our olfactory senses had been promised, this Karaage-kun delivered the gentle but unmistakable rich flavor of corn soup. There was nothing forceful or artificial-feeling about it, just a comforting, enticing flavor profile that smoothly accentuated the meaty notes of the chicken with those of sweet corn.

Just how happy were we with the Corn Soup Karaage-kun? So happy that we immediately bought another box, since we were absolutely certain knew we’d be craving more after we finished the first pack.

▼ Buying just one would be a mistake.

With the Corn Soup Karaage-kun priced at 298 yen (US$1.90), we also had room in our budget for another collaboration between Lawson and Asakuma, this one a 248-yen roll cake reimagining of the purin (custard pudding) Asakuma serves.

Nagoya is famous for the quality of its eggs, and their rich sweetness, with a touch of bitterness from the ribbon and drizzle of caramel sauce, make for an excellent dessert

Really, the only downside here is that these items aren’t available nationwide, so if you want to try them, you’ll need to head to a Lawson in Aichi, Shizuoka, Gifu, Toyama, Ishikawa, or Fukui Prefecture, or to participating stores in Mie or Fukui Prefecture. On the plus side, that means you’ll also be able to try the other Tokai/Hokuriku foods Lawson has in those regions right now, like the chicken cutlet sandwich produced in cooperation with Nagoya chicken wing specialty restaurant Furaibo.

And hey, if this gives you an excuse to combine travel and fried chicken, two of the finest things in life, then that sounds like a win-win to us.

title: Ohaw? Ruibe? Pocche? While traveling in Japan’s north, we try Ainu cuisine for the first time
description: Taste-testing the northern frontier of local foods in Japan. Just about every corner of Japan has some special food it’s famous for, and if you head up to the country’s northern tip, Hokkaido Prefecture, there are several. Travelers often arrive in Hokkaido licking their lips as they look forward to some of the country’s best […]
content:
Taste-testing the northern frontier of local foods in Japan.

Just about every corner of Japan has some special food it’s famous for, and if you head up to the country’s northern tip, Hokkaido Prefecture, there are several. Travelers often arrive in Hokkaido licking their lips as they look forward to some of the country’s best salmon roe, sea urchin, and crab, plus delicious miso ramen, soup curry, and all sorts of cheeses and dairy desserts.

But on our recent visit to Hokkaido, the most memorable things we ate were the ones we hadn’t ever heard of before this trip: ohaw, ruibe, and pocche.

If you’re an experienced eater of Japanese cuisine yet don’t recognize any of those, don’t fell like you’ve got to turn in your foodie card. All of those dishes come from the culture of the Ainu, the indigenous people who populated Hokkaido before the arrival of Japanese settlers and the region’s absorption into Japan. Though Hokkaido’s Ainu population is far smaller than it used to be, cultural centers like Akanko Ainu Kotan, near the shore of Lake Akanko, help to preserve Ainu cultural traditions and share them with visitors.

In addition to a theater with traditional dance performances and shops selling handicrafts, Akanko Ainu Kotan also has restaurants where you can try Ainu dishes, and with our visit coming right around launch time, we decided to check out the eatery Marukibune.

▼ 丸木舟 = Marukibune

After sitting down, we opened up the menu and took a look. While such standard dishes as soy sauce broth ramen and curry rice are available, we wanted a literal taste of Ainu culture, so that’s what we gravitated towards…

…and for our first step into this new-to-us food frontier, we selected the yuk kam ohaw.

Breaking that down linguistically, ohaw is a kind of stew made with fish or other animal stock and kelp. Kam ohaw means that there’s meat in the stew, and yuk indicates that the meat here is venison.

Our ohaw also contained root vegetables and wild garlic.

It looked very different from the sort of soups common to mainstream Japanese cooking, and we braced ourselves for something that could possibly be an acquired taste. That apprehension turned out to be unnecessary though, as we found it immediately delicious.

Despite the generous portion of venison, there was no gaminess at all to the flavor profile, which was instead fortifying yet simple and comforting. It was so good that we think we might find ourselves craving a bowl of ohaw once the winter chill sets in later this year.

Next up: parimomo ruibe.

Ruibe is the Ainu equivalent to sashimi, but with a few key differences. First, ruibe is prepared, and served, frozen. Second, while conventional sashimi consists pretty much entirely of saltwater seafood, ruibe is made with freshwater fish as well. In our case, parimomo is the Ainu word for the fish called Ezo ugui in Japanese (whose scientific name is Pseudaspius sachalinensis), a relative of the freshwater minnow.

Marukibune catches its Ezo ugui from Lake Kussharoko, which isn’t too far away from the restaurant, so it’s fresh and flavorful, with a sweetness that comes to a clean finish. The mouthfeel of the frozen fish slices, and the sensation of the texture changing as they thawed as we chewed, took a little getting used to, but made for an enjoyably stimulating change of pace from regular sashimi.

We also ordered a kotandon. This is a donburi (rice bowl) topped with strips of grilled pork, wild garlic, onion, and egg, flavored with a salty sweet marinade.

To be honest, we’re not sure exactly how traditional the kotandon is. In addition to being part of Akanko Ainu Kotan’s name, kotan is the Ainu word for a village or community. It seems like the kotandon might be a more modern fusion concession to visitors to Akanko Ainu Kotan who want something that’s a nod to Ainu culture but isn’t going to feel too challenging. None of that changes the fact, though, that this is a very tasty rice bowl, and one that just about anyone will probably enjoy.

And last, we ordered a pocche set.

That might look like a plate of cookies accompanying our cup of tea, but pocche are actually preserved potatoes. Hokkaido gets very cold in winter, and pocche are traditionally made by leaving potatoes outside until they freeze, then bringing them inside to thaw, and repeating the process enough times for fermentation to take place.

So rather than a dessert, pocche were actually a way to make sure the entire potato harvest could get eaten. They have a chewy texture but no sweetness beyond that which you’d find in a regular potato. We can’t really say they tasted particularly good, but they didn’t taste bad either, and they’re an interesting way to experience hands-on one way that the Ainu culture turned the harsh conditions of Hokkaido’s winter weather into a positive.

As for prices, our ohaw was 1,200 yen (US$7.50 yen), the ruibe 1,100 yen, the kotandon (which also came with a side of ruibe) 2,600 yen, and the pocche set 1,100 yen. Taking the portion sizes into account, those prices are a little on the high side, but it was money well spent for such a unique meal.

After eating, it’s also well worth your time to take a look at the rest of Akanko Ainu Kotan too.

We especially recommend the Ikor Theater, which hosts three different traditional storytelling dance performances.

Even without a reservation, we were able to catch the Ainu Ancient Ceremonial Dance program, which presents an inaw, a ceremonial tool mean to form a connection between performers and the kamuy (Ainu gods). The dances aren’t flashy, but seated in the theater, with the light of open-flame torches illuminating the dancers and singers, we were comfortably mesmerized for the 30 minutes the performance lasts.

As an added bonus, the nearby Lake Akanko is quite beautiful too, whether you’re admiring the scenery from the shore of from the deck of one of the boats offering cruises for day trippers.

So if you’re looking to broaden not only your cultural knowledge, but also your palate, while you’re in Hokkaido, stop on by Akanko Ainu Kotan and Marukibune.

title: Narita Airport Transit & Stay Program returns after six years with free tours and festival experiences
description: Immerse yourself in a lesser-known side of Japan, minutes away from the famous international airport.  Narita City in Tokyo’s neighbouring Chiba Prefecture tends to be overlooked as a travel destination, with a lot of overseas visitors bypassing it on their way in and out of the country through Narita Airport. The area around the airport […]
content:
Immerse yourself in a lesser-known side of Japan, minutes away from the famous international airport. 

Narita City in Tokyo’s neighbouring Chiba Prefecture tends to be overlooked as a travel destination, with a lot of overseas visitors bypassing it on their way in and out of the country through Narita Airport. The area around the airport really is worth exploring, though, as it retains a traditional charm with historic shrines and temples, a famous Edo-style traditional shopping street, and lots of special workshops and experiences for tourists.

To help visitors explore these charms, Narita Airport is bringing back its special free guided tours, which were introduced in 2015 but suspended due to the COVID-19 pandemic. Designed for transit passengers and foreign tourists staying around the airport, the “Narita Airport Transit & Stay Program” will officially restart on 1 October, after a six-year absence, with English-speaking volunteer guides providing free tours and an additional paid “Plus” series, for special experiences that reveal a deeper side of the area.

There are six free guided tours:

▼ Narita City (3-hour tour)

This tour takes you to Naritasan Shinshoji, a temple with 1,000 years of history, and the Omotesando shopping street, where you can pick up souvenirs and snacks at traditional stores.

▼ Naritasan Shinshoji is 25 minutes by train from Narita Airport.

▼ Katori City (5-hour tour)

Here you’ll find a riverside town with a beautiful traditional atmosphere, where you can take part in Sawara Hariko, a traditional paper-mache craft local to the area.

▼ Katori is 41 minutes by train from Narita Airport.

▼ Tako (4-hour tour)

Famous for its rice, this town boasts a beautiful green landscape and rural scenery, which you can easily explore by renting an electric-assist bicycle.

▼ Tako is 23 minutes by train from Narita Airport.

▼ Shibayama (4-hour tour)

Two of the highlights on this tour are a visit to the Museum of Aeronautical Sciences and a home-style buffet lunch, with a wide variety of local ingredients, on weekdays.

▼ Shibayama is 26 minutes by train from Narita Airport.

▼ Sakae (5-hour tour)

Slip into a yukata and step back in time at a beautiful open-air museum called Boso no Mura (“Boso Village”).

▼ Sakae is 27 minutes by train from Narita Airport

▼ Kozaki (6-hour tour)

Dubbed the “village of fermentation”, this part of Chiba prides itself on brewed and fermented products, with two sake breweries in the area, as well as miso stores and bakeries that use natural yeast made from sake lees (a byproduct of the sake-making process).

A visit to Kozaki Shrine is another highlight of the tour, and it’s said to be a good place for travelers to pray for safe journeys as it’s home to the guardian deity of aviation, transportation, and industry.

▼ Kozaki is roughly 31 minutes by train from Narita Airport.

Though the guided tours are free, participants need to cover their own expenses such as transportation, meals and admission fees. As for the paid Transit & Stay Program, there are currently nine to choose from, including a one-hour brewery tour and tasting for 1,000 yen (US$6.31)…

▼ … a knife-forging experience (4 hours, from 32,800 yen)…

…and entry to the World Boshuriken Tournament, where you can dress in a ninja costume and try out some ninja techniques for yourself (5.5 hours, 23,800 yen).

▼ What’s likely to really draw tourists, though, is the chance to participate in a local festival.

Pulling a festival float is usually only reserved for people who live in the neighbourhoods where the festival is being held, so this is a rare opportunity to immerse yourself in the culture and rub shoulders with the locals.

The first festival-focused tour to be offered is the Otaiyasai Festival on 5 September, which is being treated as a pre-official launch event. Taking around five hours and priced from 15,800 yen, this tour takes place at the Sogo Reido temple, which is half an hour by train from the airport.

Those pressed for time can enjoy a shorter two-hour float-pulling experience at the Narita Gion Festival on Omotesando Street from 8-11 July 2027…

… while those wanting maximum festival immersion can stay overnight during the Narita Gion Festival, with the float-pulling experience followed by time in a special viewing room at the Waqoo Naritasan Monzen hotel.

One night’s accommodation at Waqoo Naritasan Monzen with breakfast and dinner are also included in the deal, all for 84,000 yen.

These tours prove that the area around Narita Airport really is home to some great hidden gems. So if you’re passing through the region, or looking for something to do during a long layover, these Transit & Stay tours are a great way to explore outside the airport and experience a lesser-known side of Japan with the help of a local.

Reservations for the free tours open on 15 September and can be made here, while the paid tours are available to purchase now from this site.

title: Japan’s double-decker portable rice cooker/bento maker is better than ever with new version
description: Now there’s even more to be thankful to Thanko for. Japanese gadget maker Thanko has repeatedly shown its knack for innovations to be grateful for, but the company’s best idea of all is arguably its One-Person Rice Cooker Series. These compact kitchen appliances let you cook enough rice for a single serving, and their easy […]
content:
Now there’s even more to be thankful to Thanko for.

Japanese gadget maker Thanko has repeatedly shown its knack for innovations to be grateful for, but the company’s best idea of all is arguably its One-Person Rice Cooker Series. These compact kitchen appliances let you cook enough rice for a single serving, and their easy portability means that you can take them with you and cook your rice at your office desk or wherever else you need to be in the early part of the day, letting you enjoy freshly steamed rice once your lunch break comes around.

Of course, even Japanese people don’t eat just rice for lunch, so Thanko also makes two-tier one-person rice cookers. The bottom section is for cooking the rice, and the steam that rises from it is channeled into the upper section stacked on top of it, where it can cook, reheat, or thaw whatever vegetables, dumplings, curry roux, or other side dishes that you’re pairing with your rice.

With restaurant prices rising, Thanko says it’s seeing even higher demand than usual for its one-person rice cookers, and so the company’s designers have made a few improvements. First, they’ve managed to make the cooking process even speedier, and it now takes just 14 minutes to have a batch of rice ready to eat. They’ve added a timer function that will automatically start the cooking process one, two, or three hours after you set it. This new feature was added in order to make the one-person rice cooker easier to use with brown rice, which benefits from a longer soaking period than white rice, and thus increase the variety of meals that can be made with the device.

The one-person rice cooker is even a handy option for car camping, since it’ll work with vehicle power outlets as long as they put out at a voltage of at least 300 watts.

And yes, it’s still as compact as ever and easily breaks down into its component parts for easy cleaning.

▼ The parts shown at the bottom left are even dishwasher-safe.

The new and improved double-decker one-person rice cooker is priced at 8,980 yen (US$56) and just went on sale this week through the Thanko online store here.

title: Wait, some Shinkansen trains already have private booths that only cost 1,500 yen for an hour?
description: High-speed serenity has been low-key available on the Shinkansen for a long time with hardly anyone noticing it. A new Supreme Class is coming to Shinkansen trains this fall, offering luxurious private cabins for those with deep pockets. It turns out, though, that some bullet trains in Japan have quietly had available private booths for […]
content:
High-speed serenity has been low-key available on the Shinkansen for a long time with hardly anyone noticing it.

A new Supreme Class is coming to Shinkansen trains this fall, offering luxurious private cabins for those with deep pockets. It turns out, though, that some bullet trains in Japan have quietly had available private booths for years, and at very affordable prices.

If you’re wondering how this service has managed to escape the attention of so many travelers in Japan, it’s because the private booth is only offered on certain trains, and can only be reserved by certain passengers. Specifically, it’s only found on N700S-series Nozomi Shinkansen trains running on the Tokaido and Sanyo lines (i.e. between Tokyo and Fukuoka’s Hakata Station), and the booth can only be booked by passengers who’ve also purchased a regular seat in Car 7. The booth is located in the connecting area between Cars 7 and 8, and is equipped with two chairs, a counter, standard and USB power outlets, and a window so that you can watch the scenery zoom by from your private space.

You can use the booth either by yourself or with one other traveling companion, and rather than booking it for the length of your trip, it can be reserved, in 10-minute increments, for a block of time up to two hours.

So what’s the surcharge, on top of your Car 7 regular class Shinkansen ticket, to use this private booth? Hardly anything. Prices are just 200 yen (US$1.25) per 10 minutes up to a half-hour, and 300 yen per 10 minutes between 30 and 60 minutes, which works out to 600 yen for a 30-minute session or 1,500 yen for a full hour (payment is done by credit card). Things get a little pricier after that, with 90 minutes costing 2,500 yen and two hours 4,000 yen, but still, this a pretty affordable pocket of serene solitude.

Another likely reason this booth has largely escaped attention from travel fans is that, despite being available since 2022, it hasn’t been pitched to luxury travelers. In fact, JR calls it the Business Booth, and its exclusive availability to Car 7 on N700S Nozomi trains is because Car 7 is designated as the S Work car, which is promoted as being a car for passengers who need to get some work done during their ride. As such, the Business Booth isn’t outfitted with swanky interior fittings, and was primarily designed as a place where you can open up your laptop, lay out some documents, and make phone calls or hold video conferences with professional colleagues. All that said, it still remains a place you can have all to yourself for a while during your Shinkansen journey, even if all you want to do is relax.

Use of the Business Booth cannot be reserved ahead of time. Instead, after boarding you can check for/claim available time blocks via a QR code displayed at the booth’s entrance or on a pamphlet at your seat.

And, once again, the Business Booth is exclusive to N700S Nozomi trains, and if you’re looking for one, JR Central allows you to check which Shinkansen of that class are running on the current day by clicking on the button labeled ビジネスブースを搭載している今日の列車はこちら on their official website here.

title: German woman rescued from Mt. Fuji after suffering altitude sickness symptoms, hiking to peak anyway
description: Visited same medical center on way up and down the mountain. August 20 was a bad day for good judgement on Mt. Fuji. We already looked at the story of a 7-year-old Japanese boy whose dad left him to fend for himself on the side of Japan’s tallest mountain, and it turns out that on […]
content:
Visited same medical center on way up and down the mountain.

August 20 was a bad day for good judgement on Mt. Fuji. We already looked at the story of a 7-year-old Japanese boy whose dad left him to fend for himself on the side of Japan’s tallest mountain, and it turns out that on the same morning, a German woman had to be transported down from Mt. Fuji by rescue workers.

The 33-year-old woman began hiking the Fujinomiya Trail on the morning of August 19, beginning at the trail’s fifth station. In the afternoon, the woman, along with a traveling companion, reached the eighth station, representing a rise in elevation from 2,400 meters to 3,250 meters (7,874 feet to 10,663 feet). However, by this time the woman was suffering from altitude sickness symptoms, which typically include dizziness, fatigue, and nausea. After undergoing a medical examination at the eighth station’s medical center, the woman secured accommodations in a mountain hut and rested through the night.

The next morning, before dawn, the woman got back on the trail and pressed on to the summit, an ascent of a further 526 meters that, according to the official Mt. Fuji climbing website, takes around two hours under ordinary conditions. She eventually made it to the peak, but she would not be able to make it home under her own power.

It’s not clear whether it started happening during her climb to the summit or on her way back down, but at some point, the woman began to once again suffer from altitude sickness symptoms. She was able to make her way back down to the eighth station, but felt so unwell that she again visited the medical center, where it was deemed too dangerous for her to continue the descent on her own. A doctor called for members of the Shizuoka Prefectural Police’s mountain rescue team, who were posted near the ninth station, to come and assist the woman, which they did by transporting her in a bulldozer back down to the fifth station, where the trail meets up with the road network, after which she was transferred into the custody of paramedics who took her to the hospital for examination and treatment.

Following the German woman’s rescue, the Shizuoka Prefectural Police issued a statement reminding hikers, and not for the first time, that if they feel any concern about their physical condition while on the trail, they should call of their ascent.

The details of the woman’s first examination at the eighth station haven’t been made publicly available at the time of this writing, so it can’t be said whether or not her pre-dawn hike to the summit on August 20 was in defiance of the medical staff’s recommendations. However, much like with the incident involving a 99-year-old Japanese woman who needed to be rescued on the mountain last month, should you suffer from injuries or symptoms that require you to rest overnight in a mountain hut, it might be best to take that as a sign that your body isn’t currently up for a hike all the way to the top of Mt. Fuji, and that once you’re able to move under your own power again, down, not up, should probably be the direction you’re walking.

title: KFC Japan unveils new Tsukimi collection that takes moon-viewing to extreme levels
description: Eggs run wild for this ever-evolving Japanese tradition. As we head towards autumn in Japan, the change of seasons brings with it one of the country’s most famous seasonal events: Tsukimi, or “Moon Viewing”. Traditionally, Tsukimi, which takes place on 25 September this year, involves seasonal foods like round dango rice dumplings, which people enjoy […]
content:
Eggs run wild for this ever-evolving Japanese tradition.

As we head towards autumn in Japan, the change of seasons brings with it one of the country’s most famous seasonal events: Tsukimi, or “Moon Viewing”. Traditionally, Tsukimi, which takes place on 25 September this year, involves seasonal foods like round dango rice dumplings, which people enjoy while gazing at the moon. With modern lifestyles these days, though, the tradition has evolved somewhat, with fast food chains now adding limited-edition Tsukimi items to the menu, usually featuring a fried egg, due to the way the egg resembles the full moon.

One of the collections we look forward to most every year is the “Torori Tsukimi” series (“torori” means “melty”) from KFC Japan. This year the chain is going all out with the moon-viewing, giving us five limited-edition menu items, three of which are marked as new, with four containing a fried-egg-style omelette filled with a rich and melty egg-yolk sauce.

▼ “新” means “New”

Starting with the more familiar items, which are so popular they’ve become something of a standard release every year, we have the Torori Tsukimi Filet Burger (590 yen [US$3.95]) and the Torori Tsukimi Twister (490 yen), both of which get an eggy upgrade.

▼ The Twister adds teriyaki sauce and mayonnaise for even more melty enjoyment.

The two new burgers take things a step further, with “Kobore Tartar” (“kobore” means “spilling out”) and wafu katsu (“Japanese-style cutlet”) being key ingredients in addition to the egg.

▼ Torori Tsukimi Wafu Katsu Burger Kobore Tartar (640 yen)

▼ Torori Triple Tsukimi Wafu Katsu Burger Kobore Tartar (990 yen)

This towering burger stacks three eggs on top of each other, creating what KFC describes as “an egg-filled burger with plenty of visual impact”. Though the chain bills this as a new release, it was available at seven KFC locations last year (we know because our own reporter Mr Sato tried it). Due to glowing reviews, the chain decided to roll it out at all its branches around Japan this year, so more people can enjoy the triple tower of moon-viewing enjoyment.

▼ Rounding out the collection is the Omochi to Noko (“rich”) Custard no Tsukimi Pie (320 yen, or 450 yen for two)

The dessert also gets an eggier upgrade to qualify as a new release this year, with 20 percent more custard filling compared to its last appearance. The custard is made with Madagascar vanilla beans and is paired with a chewy mochi filling, all wrapped up in crispy pie pastry.

This year’s campaign also comes with a deliciously over-the-top concept video, starring T.M.Revolution frontman Takanori Nishikawa as “T.M.G. Revolution”, with “T.M.G.” standing for “tamago” or “egg”.

The new 30-second video will be released on 26 August, alongside a commercial called “Eggs Run Wild”, starring Japanese model and television personality Shiori Sato.

KFC’s new Tsukimi collection proves you can never have too much egg during moon-viewing season, and it’ll be available while stocks last from 26 August.

title: Masturbatory aid maker Tenga releases officially licensed anime versions in Japan and U.S.

content:
Hey, look who’s coming to Tenga!

Fans of Panty & Stocking with Garterbelt had to wait a long time for a follow-up to the anime series’ initial 2010 season. It wasn’t until 15 years later, in the summer of 2025, that New Panty & Stocking with Garterbelt finally arrived.

However, with the sequel series having consisted of just 13 episodes, fans of the franchise are once again going to have to be patient for their anime-viewing desires to be fulfilled. That doesn’t mean that they’re going to need to practice restraint in all aspects of their lives, though, as Japanese masturbatory aid manufacturer Tenga is now selling officially licensed New Panty & Stocking with Garterbelt versions of its products.

If you were to go strictly by the art style, Panty & Stocking with Garterbelt might seem like an odd choice for a partnership with Tenga. The series’ character designs aren’t particularly sexy or sexualized, especially by the standards of the anime industry where building at least a little titillation into a series’ aesthetic is generally the default strategy. There are literally hundreds of recent anime series that are much more focused on getting viewers in the mood for some self-love.

However, despite the nature of its business, Tenga doesn’t really try to market its products as being sexy in and of themselves. Instead, the company’s aim is to try to remove the awkward stigmatization of doing the wash by hand, so to speak. Similarly, Panty & Stocking with Garterbelt’ s protagonist sisters, demon-fighting angels Panty and Stocking, are shown to be unabashed about indulging their lustful or kinky urges, and that appears to be the thematic synergy that the collaboration is looking to harness.

In addition to the New Panty and Stocking with Garterbelt Special Collaboration Tenga Cup masturbatory aid pictured above, there’s also the New Panty and Stocking with Garterbelt Special Collaboration Tenga Tissue Case.

This, of course, is designed for extracting tissues, not inserting bodily fluids. Tenga describes it as a “divine decoration for your room,” and it could technically be used for entirely chaste purposes, making it equally useful for those looking to blow their nose or their wad.

▼ Size-wise, the tissue case is significantly larger than the Tenga cup.

Panty & Stocking with Garterbelt famously takes a lot of its art and humor styles from American adult animation, and these items made their debut at last month’s Anime Expo convention in Los Angeles. They’re now available for order through both the U.S. and Japan Tenga online shops, here and here, with the cup priced at US$13.99 or 1,200 yen, and the tissue case US$34.99 or 3,850 yen. Just make sure not to mix them up with Tenga’s bug repellant dispensers.

title: The Japanese government is ending its Cool Japan Fund program
description: Cool Japan’s mission has been accomplished, but not because of Cool Japan. Back in 2013, the Japanese government’s Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry had an idea. What if they created a program to promote the appealing aspects of Japanese culture, including pop culture, to people around the world? This wasn’t going to be a […]
content:
Cool Japan’s mission has been accomplished, but not because of Cool Japan.

Back in 2013, the Japanese government’s Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry had an idea. What if they created a program to promote the appealing aspects of Japanese culture, including pop culture, to people around the world? This wasn’t going to be a stuffy, overly academic way of looking at Japanese culture, either, but rather a way of spreading the word about all the ways Japan is cool.

And thus was born the Cool Japan Fund, which describes itself as “a public-private fund with the aim of contributing to the sustainable growth of Japan’s economy through the expansion of overseas demand and supply of attractive products and services unique to Japanese lifestyle and culture.” Entertainment content such as anime, manga, and pop music were among the areas to be championed, along with food, fashion, technology, and tourism attractions.

With the rapid rise in global enthusiasm for Japanese stuff over the last decade and a half, one might expect the Cool Japan Fund to have been a huge success, but that’s actually not the case at all. Instead, in 2025 the Cool Japan Fund’s deficit grew to a staggering 54 billion yen (US$340 million), and now the Japanese government is ready to effectively shut the program down.

Inside sources have leaked to multiple media organizations that the Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry’s upcoming 2027 budget proposal will not be asking for any funds for the Cool Japan Fund. This would remove the program’s ability to invest in any new projects, and since investing is pretty much all the Cool Japan Fund does, by extension, this would terminate the program, since the chance of the it somehow rising out of being 54 billion yen in the red while in a dormant state is negligible.

▼ We don’t know how many sofas there are in the ministry’s offices, but there probably don’t collectively contain enough dropped change to balance the Cool Japan Fund’s budget.

As for how the Cool Japan Fund got itself into such a dire situation, the program has been criticized for picking poor partners for more than a decade, with detractors saying Cool Japan was in the habit of providing vague, unhelpful support to projects with poor prospects. Among the most recent embarrassments is the Cool Japan Fund’s backing of Junglia Okinawa, a dinosaur-themed amusement park/resort that opened in Okinawa last year. Almost immediately, Junglia was mocked by Japanese travelers for its high prices and dull attractions, and foreign tourists, who were charged more for admission due to Junglia’s two-tier ticket prices, seemed even less interested in visiting.

The irony here is that while the Cool Japan Fund was flailing and floundering, Japan still managed to build a reputation as one of the coolest countries in the world. Global interest in Japanese media franchises, food, and travel has skyrocketed, just not for the specific partners that the Cool Japan Fund was pushing. Part of that recent boom is, undeniably, stems from the yen’s recent weakness making Japanese products and vacations suddenly very affordable for people from other countries, and arguably some of the Cool Japan Fund’s early swings-and-misses might have performed better had they taken place with today’s exchange rates. The bigger takeaway, though, is that Japanese businesses and private-sector organizations have shown themselves to be perfectly capable of showing the world the cool stuff they have without the Cool Japan Fund’s help.

So in an odd way, while the Cool Japan Fund itself didn’t accomplish the goal is set out to, that goal has still been accomplished. In a time when cost of living increases are making middle and lower-class Japanese households tighten their belts, it’s for the best that the Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry stop throwing taxpayer money at a program whose help isn’t needed, and whose efforts probably wouldn’t be very helpful anyway.

In the case of Japan, it has led to things like the tradition of yoshoku (Western dishes adapted […]
content:
A rare East-meets-West tea ceremony in a seldom seen tearoom.

A country’s culture is often deep and never-ending, always with new facets to explore, but the point where two cultures meet and blend is no less fascinating. In the case of Japan, it has led to things like the tradition of yoshoku (Western dishes adapted for Japanese tastes), and modern musical groups like Wagakki Band, which blends rock with traditional Japanese instruments. The fusion of Japanese and Western cultures stretches into many fields, and one of these can be seen in Kyoto. Within the city, a landmark that bridges these two worlds exists as Hotel Chorakukan.

Built in 1909 during the Meiji era (1868–1912) by wealthy tobacco industrialist Kichibei Murai, Chourakukan was originally designed as a grand villa to entertain foreign diplomats, nobility, and prominent global figures. Its construction reflected an era when Japan was rapidly modernizing and actively welcoming the West, with its outer appearance utilizing a brick and stone-heavy design characteristically found in European countries rather than the more wooden structures found in traditional Japanese architecture. Over a century later, the mansion still serves as an elegant venue where traditional Japanese heritage and European luxury harmonize.

To celebrate this legacy, the hotel will host the annual Art Festival in Chourakukan 2026 on September 27. In its fifth installment, the festival aims to introduce the history, architectural beauty, and guest-receiving traditions of Chorakukan to the public. Under this year’s theme of Architecture and Hospitality Culture, the one-day event offers a variety of cultural, artistic, and culinary experiences.

While there are several activities to do at the festival, from incense making to enjoying a French dinner course, one of the main highlights of the festival is the opportunity for general visitors to attend a special Tea Serving Experience (known as “teicha”) in Chorakuan, a magnificent third-floor tearoom that is usually kept strictly private.

Teicha is the formal act of preparing matcha and entertaining guests and can be seen to be a significantly shorter and more streamlined version of a full-scale, formal tea gathering (“chaji”). A chaji could last anywhere up to four hours, following a strict sequence of events and ceremonies, and participants are expected to hold a deep knowledge of the complex etiquette involved. Teicha, on the other hand, usually lasts in the range of 30 to 45 minutes, with the host preparing matcha alongside a seasonal confection without the ritual.

The tearoom Chorakuan is built as a replica of Zangetsutei, a famous historic tearoom originating from Omotesenke, one of the three main historical schools of Japanese tea ceremony. While classical tearooms emphasize simplicity, Chorakuan features vibrant stained-glass windows depicting spring cherry blossoms and autumn foliage.

The event will be held over six sessions between 10:30 a.m. and 5:15 p.m., with each being approximately 45 minutes. These sessions will accommodate ten guests per session, and advance reservation is required, making for a very exclusive experience. Tickets cost 2,500 yen (US$16), which includes admission to the Art Festival, or if you happen to have already picked up a ticket to the festival, the tea experience will cost an additional 2,000 yen.

After September 27, the tearoom Chorakuan will once again close its doors to the public, until the next special event comes around. Enjoying matcha served alongside seasonal sweets in a traditional room illuminated by Western stained glass offers an unforgettable East-meets-West experience, so keep your eyes out for the next opportunity if you happen to miss out. Or try out other avenues of mixed cultures by rocking a denim kimono or making your own sushi burgers.

title: 7-year-old boy left behind on Mt. Fuji by his own dad
description: Police not pleased with plan of leaving elementary schooler unattended for hours on Japan’s tallest mountain. “This summer, I hiked Mt. Fuji with my dad!” sounds like a pretty cool opening for a kid’s how-I-spent-my-summer-vacation essay. The composition gets less heartwarming, though, if it concludes with “And then I got to meet some policemen after […]
content:
Police not pleased with plan of leaving elementary schooler unattended for hours on Japan’s tallest mountain.

“This summer, I hiked Mt. Fuji with my dad!” sounds like a pretty cool opening for a kid’s how-I-spent-my-summer-vacation essay. The composition gets less heartwarming, though, if it concludes with “And then I got to meet some policemen after he abandoned me on the side of the tallest mountain in Japan.”

And yet, that’s exactly what happened to a 7-year-old boy from Nagoya on Thursday. Early that morning, the boy, his 48-year-old father, and his older brother (a first-year middle school student, making him either 12 or 13 years old) had started their hike up the Fujinomiya Trail. At somewhere around the trail’s sixth of 10 stations on the way to the summit, the younger child became fussy, complaining that he was tired.

At this point, the obvious options would be either to offer some words of encouragement to the tuckered-out tyke, take a break so he could rest and recover his stamina, or, perhaps, to simply accept that taking a 7-year-old on an attempt to summit Mt. Fuji was a flawed plan from the start, and so head home. Instead, Dad decided to tell his younger son “Wait here,” after which he and the older boy continued hiking towards the top of the mountain.

It’s not like the summit was just a hop, skip, and a jump away from where the dad abandoned his flesh and blood, either. According to the Mt. Fuji Climbing Official Website, it takes a little over five hours to hike from the Fujinomiya Trail’s sixth station to the peak, and slightly more than two and a half hours to walk back down there from the top. That means the dad was counting on a 7-year-old to sit tight and keep himself safe on the mountain for at least seven and a half hours, and likely longer once you factor in any time spent by the dad and older brother on rest breaks, taking photos, or admiring the view at the summit.

▼ Approximate ascent hiking times on the Fujinomiya Trail

Thankfully, the younger kid didn’t end up having to do that. At around 7:40 in the morning, a worker at a mountain hut near the sixth station spotted the unattended boy sitting by himself on a bench. The worker invited the boy inside the hut and let him take shelter there while the police were contacted. Once officers arrived, they were able to determine the father’s identity and get in contact with him, at which time he was near the trail’s eighth station, and told him to come back and get his kid.

It’s not clear exactly how long the boy was left unattended for, but, once again going by the Mt. Fuji Climbing Official Website’s estimates, it’s a roughly three-hour hike from the trail’s sixth station to the eighth, meaning he likely abandoned his son sometime around 4:30 in the morning.

Thankfully, the boy was unharmed and was safely reunited with his father. However, when the mountain hut worker found the boy, rain was falling and fog was starting to gather. It’s not known what the weather was like when the father left his son behind, but conditions can rapidly and unpredictably change on Mt. Fuji, sometimes leading to rapid deteriorations of visibility, footing, and other safety factors.

“Even if it means having to give up on climbing the mountain together, leaving a child behind is unacceptable” officers told the father, who, at least, seems remorseful, saying “I made a rash decision, and I deeply regret it.” Following the incident, the police are calling on hikers to be conscious of the dangers of leaving a member of their party behind, reminding those taking to the trails that they should tailor their pace and ambitions to accommodate the member of their group with the lowest amount of stamina.

title: Sushi Bus: Japan’s first conveyor-belt bus lets you eat sushi while sightseeing around Tokyo
description: Jiro dreams of sushi, but he never would’ve dreamed of this. When you’re visiting Japan on a tight schedule and trying to pack as much as possible into your short time here, being able to do two things at once can be a timesaver. It can also become a weird, surreal and Japan-only experience, if […]
content:
Jiro dreams of sushi, but he never would’ve dreamed of this.

When you’re visiting Japan on a tight schedule and trying to pack as much as possible into your short time here, being able to do two things at once can be a timesaver. It can also become a weird, surreal and Japan-only experience, if the new “Sushi Bus” is anything to go by.

This unusual new attraction combines conveyor belt sushi with a sightseeing bus tour, by putting a working sushi conveyor belt on the second floor of an open-top double-decker bus to create a new experience that’s said to be the first of its kind in the world.

Developed by Sushi Bus Co. in collaboration with Willer Across, which rents out restaurant buses with onboard kitchens, this new service is as impressive as it sounds: passengers sit on the second floor of an open-top bus while sushi travels around them on a conveyor belt, allowing them to eat as they take in views of Tokyo.

▼ Yes, the sushi really will be moving around the bus.

The bus will depart from the Kajibashi Parking Lot near Tokyo Station, but unlike a conventional sightseeing tour, it won’t be travelling to a specific destination. Instead, it will go on a spin around the city, much like the conveyor belt inside it, passing famous sites while passengers enjoy all-you-can-eat sushi on the 70-minute tour.

The restaurant bus has a kitchen on the first floor, where staff prepare a variety of sushi. An elevator inside the bus transports the finished sushi to the second floor, where a staff member places it onto the conveyor belt running alongside the passenger seats.

▼ The elevator system in action.

The current plan is for the bus to have just 20 seats, so there will only be 20 diners on board. The company says this limited capacity is part of the appeal, and because the bus is so unusual, it’s likely to attract plenty of attention as it travels around Tokyo. making Shibuya Scramble Crossing, Ginza and Kaminarimon in Asakusa some of the likely contendors for sites along the yet-to-be determined route.

The Sushi Bus concept, which has been in development for roughly two and a half years, started with an April 2024 illustration of what the bus might look like.

The road to making it a reality involved a lot of testing and lateral thinking, as the companies involved had to work out a way to install a sushi conveyor belt on a moving vehicle while also dealing with the kitchen facilities and other requirements involved in operating a restaurant bus.

▼ Team members hard at work, to accomplish “a project no one had ever attempted before”.

The conveyor itself required extensive testing with Kitanihon Kako, a major Japanese manufacturer of sushi conveyor systems, to prevent sushi from falling off the belt in the case of sudden braking.

▼ This test-ride video shows how well the sushi stays on the belt, even when the bus comes to a sudden stop.

Sushi Bus says there are currently only five restaurant buses operating in Japan, all owned by Willer Group. One of the five has now been renovated to become the Sushi Bus, which is said to be the first of its kind in the world.

▼ The company says it can accommodate a variety of dietary requirements, including religious dietary restrictions, allergies and “vegitarian” requests.

The new service is currently set to begin with one bus in Tokyo, although the company hopes to eventually expand to other major tourist destinations like Osaka and Kyoto as well.

The planned price is 16,000 yen (US$101) per person, with online reservations here and five departure times scheduled each day: 11 a.m., 1 p.m., 3 p.m., 5 p.m. and 7 p.m. The bus is scheduled to begin operating in Tokyo on 10 October.

title: Ninja theme park suddenly closes in Japan, shadow warriors undone by shady real estate deals
description: If only some justice-loving shinobi had put a stop to things before Ise Ninja Kingdom had to shut down. It would seem like right now would be a great time to operate a ninja theme park in Japan. With the yen at its lowest value in decades, the country is receiving record-breaking numbers of foreign […]
content:
If only some justice-loving shinobi had put a stop to things before Ise Ninja Kingdom had to shut down.

It would seem like right now would be a great time to operate a ninja theme park in Japan. With the yen at its lowest value in decades, the country is receiving record-breaking numbers of foreign tourists, many with an interest in traditional Japanese culture, and Japan residents, with overseas travel now a much more expensive endeavor, are in need of domestic entertainment options.

And yet, Ise Ninja Kingdom, in Mie Prefecture, has suddenly closed, and it’s not clear if it will ever reopen.

▼ Ise Ninja Kingdom commercial

The park, located in the town of Ise, originally opened in 1993 as Ise Sengoku Village, referencing the Sengoku period of Japanese history, when dozens of regional samurai clans were vying for control of the country. The facility boasts a recreation of a samurai-era fortress and castle town, with activities and martial arts shows for visitors to enjoy.

The park has changed names and owners several times, and following its purchase by the Kyosei Bank Group real estate investment firm in 2016, rebranded as Ise Ninja Kingdom in 2019. Like all amusement parks, its attendance cratered during the COVID pandemic, but Ise Ninja Kingdom managed to weather the storm and avoid bankruptcy. Unfortunately, while it may have survived the public health crisis, it looks like Ise Ninja Kingdom has been undone by a business scandal.

On July 22, Ise Ninja Kingdom announced that it would be closing “for renovations,” and that the closure would be starting the very next day. The park’s website has been almost entirely erased as well, and now consists only of a top page with the text-image statement:

“Thank you for your continued patronage of Ise Ninja Kingdom. As of Thursday, July 23, 2026, the facility will be suspending operations for the purpose of renovations. We ask for the understanding of those parties who had been planning to visit. When operations resume, it will be announced through the park’s official site.”

In the month since, there has been no update, nor has there been a single statement regarding what sort of renovations are supposedly in the works or their scale. The entrance to the park has been roped off and no construction workers or equipment has been seen. Following the announcement of the closure, representatives for the park turned in the paperwork to formally withdraw from Ise’s municipal tourism promotion association as well.

▼ Roughly a week before the closure, the official Ise Ninja Kingdom ninja YouTube channel also announced that it would be “going into cold sleep,” and has not posted since.

But while the suddenness and exact manner are starling, Ise Ninja Kingdom closing down isn’t itself a shock. As mentioned above, the park was acquired in 2016 by Kyosei Bank Group. Among the company’s investment products is one called Minna de Oyasan, which translates to “Everyone as the Landlords Together.” Minna de Oyasan was touted as a sort of crowdfunding-style investment opportunity, but critics have accused it of being a gussied-up Ponzi scheme. A string of scandals involving misrepresentations of what investors’ money was being used for and noncompliance in fulfilling obligations to return investors’ money led to a lawsuit filed by nearly 1,200 plaintiffs seeking 11.4 billion yen (US$72 million) from the company.

While Ise Ninja Kingdom and its management don’t appear to have been directly involved in the alleged wrongdoings, the park’s association with Kyosei Bank Group has resulted in the shadow warrior theme park’s reputation being tarnished by the shady real estate deals. Attendance had been plummeting for the past several months, with those visitors who did walk through Ise Ninja Kingdom’s gate finding that they had the park almost entirely to themselves, and certain parts of the facility, such as some of its restaurants, not operating.

▼ A video from this past March showing a largely empty Ise Ninja Kingdom

Taking all of this into account, it certainly seems like instead of closing for “renovations,” Ise Ninja Kingdom is instead closing down until either Kyosei Bank Group’s scandal fades from people’s minds or the company can find someone else to sell it to. Neither of those are likely to happen very soon, though, if ever, so it’s good to know that there’s another samurai-era theme park in Japan that’s ramping up its offerings, not shutting them down.

title: Burger King Japan brings back its insane all-you-can-eat One Pounder Challenge
description: Can you eat more than 12 mega burgers in just 45 minutes for a chance at winning the national final? Fast-food enthusiasts, please prepare yourselves: Burger King Japan’s legendary One Pounder Challenge is back for its third and final round in 2026, and it’s as gloriously tasty as ever. The star of this all-you-can-eat extravaganza […]
content:
Can you eat more than 12 mega burgers in just 45 minutes for a chance at winning the national final?

Fast-food enthusiasts, please prepare yourselves: Burger King Japan’s legendary One Pounder Challenge is back for its third and final round in 2026, and it’s as gloriously tasty as ever.

The star of this all-you-can-eat extravaganza is the monstrous Dirty The One Pounder, packing four flame-grilled 100 percent beef patties, four slices of rich cheddar cheese, pickles, onions, and a special garlic mayo sauce. Individually priced at 2,490 yen (US$15.70), or as set for 2,790 yen, and clocking in at 1,656 calories and 527 grams (1.16 pounds) per burger, it’s both a test for your stomach and your heart.

The event runs for seven days, from August 28 to September 3, with daily sessions being held at 2:30 p.m., 4:00 p.m., 5:30 p.m., and 7:00 p.m., and each catering to small groups of just six to eight participants. It’s taking place at a Whoppering 90 stores nationwide, from Hokkaido to Fukuoka, including a brand-new debut at Aeon Mall Morioka-Minami in Iwate. Although do note that the branches at Tokyo and Kyoto Racetracks, and also Kansai International Airport Terminal 1, are not participating in this event or selling the jumbo burger.

After the clock starts, you have 45 minutes to eat as much as you can. The timer is strict, and your last order must be placed at the 30-minute mark. A rotation system is enforced, so after you are presented with your first burger, small order of French fries, and medium drink, you must have completely finished your current portion of any item before you are able to order another. However, you don’t need to finish your fries to order another burger, just wolf that burger down, and another stack of beef will be sent your way.

Participation in the event costs 4,900 yen, and tickets must be purchased online in advance via the official booking site here. Sales opened on August 19 on a first-come, first-served basis, and this event is known to sell out quickly, so you’ll want to grab your ticket as quickly as possible. Every participant takes home exclusive merchandise: a limited One Pounder T-shirt, an original Burger King pouch, a One Pounder sticker, and an event sticker.

You should show up at least five minutes before your scheduled slot, and be sure to keep your ticket secure. As you’re shovelling what feels like could be an entire cow down your throat in an attempt to smash the top record from the challenge back in June of an astonishing 12 burgers (over 19,000 calories), it’s important to pace yourself and eat safely.

However, if you do happen to accomplish becoming one of the top three eaters nationwide, you will also receive an invitation to the grand One Pounder Challenge 2026 Final in Tokyo at the end of the year.

If you’ve got your ticket in hand, get those stomachs warmed up and ready to feast, but if you’ve missed out this time, you should also train those finger muscles in order to snap up the ticket for the next all-you-can-eat showdown before your competition.

title: You can send your suitcase from Tokyo to Kyoto on the Shinkansen for same-day delivery… but it’ll cost you
description: Overlooked luggage-forwarding service will become easier to use this autumn, especially for tourists staying in private rentals like Airbnbs. A ride on the Shinkansen is one of the most enjoyable ways to get around Japan, but the only downside is having to deal with your luggage during the journey. There does appear to be light […]
content:
Overlooked luggage-forwarding service will become easier to use this autumn, especially for tourists staying in private rentals like Airbnbs.

A ride on the Shinkansen is one of the most enjoyable ways to get around Japan, but the only downside is having to deal with your luggage during the journey. There does appear to be light at the end of the tunnel, though, as companies are now coming up with new services that allow travellers to send their suitcases to their destinations so they can travel hands-free in ways that are easier than ever before.

One of the newest services is “Luggage Express”, a luggage delivery service from JTB that uses the Tokaido Shinkansen to transport bags between Tokyo, Kyoto and Osaka. First launched in November last year, Luggage Express remains relatively unknown compared to other more widely used road-based luggage forwarding services like Takkyubin, provided by Yamato Transport.

However, unlike Yamato and other truck-based providers, who generally offer next-day delivery between Tokyo, Kyoto and Osaka, Luggage Express has speed on its side. By using the Tokaido bullet train service, Luggage Express can get your bags there on the very same day, which remains rare for such a long-distance delivery route.

Same-day delivery makes luggage forwarding even more stress-free, as you don’t have to pack a change of clothes into a day bag while waiting for your luggage to arrive the next day. Plus, you don’t have to waste time frantically looking for an elevator to make your connection in Tokyo’s labyrinthine stations, only to give up and take the stairs.

Previously, using Luggage Express wasn’t entirely simple, as pickup and dropoff was only available at hotels, airports, and three train stations – Tokyo, Kyoto and Osaka – with a prior online booking. However, a new partnership announced this week is about to make it easier for foreign tourists to use – from September, Luggage Express will be integrated with Bounce, a global luggage-storage platform that has thousands of convenient locations in Japan.

By teaming up with Bounce, the same-day service opens up luggage-forwarding to a wider range of tourists, including those staying at private accommodation rentals like Airbnbs. Many luggage-forwarding services require a hotel address with a staffed check-in desk for delivery, so the new tie-up with Bounce lets people in vacation rentals forward their luggage to a nearby Bounce location for pickup and dropoff.

Travellers will be able to arrange delivery in multiple languages through the multilingual Bounce app by selecting their desired Bounce dropoff location, delivery date, destination and number of bags. Payment is also completed through the app, so for those using the Tokyo–Kyoto route, all you have to do is take your luggage to the dropoff point by 10 a.m. and it will be delivered to your selected hotel or Bounce branch from 6 p.m. that same day.

There are some caveats to using the service, however, with the main one being the cost. As it turns out, same-day delivery doesn’t come cheap, as the regular service (dropoff before 10 a.m. and pick-up/delivery from 8:00 p.m.) costs 13,200 yen (US$83). The express service (dropoff by 10 a.m. and pick-up/delivery from 6:00 p.m. or dropoff by 12 p.m. and pick-up/delivery from 8:00 p.m) costs 16,500 yen per item.

With the cost of a regular-season reserved-seat Nozomi Shinkansen ticket from Tokyo to Kyoto costing around 14,170 yen, the same-day delivery service does seem steep, but with Bounce taking care of the handoff and JTB looking after the delivery infrastructure and Shinkansen-based transport, the cost covers all the behind-the-scenes logistics to provide customers with one of the fastest delivery services in the country.

Like many other luggage-forwarding services, delivery is limited to eligible locations, so you’ll need to check the site for information on hotel requirements and Bounce stores, including opening hours.

If you’re travelling on a budget, Bounce can also help you out as it offers next day luggage delivery at a considerably lower price, sending your luggage for you via Yamato Transport. For Tokyo to Kyoto, for instance, you can send a large suitcase for around 4,900 yen, which is slightly higher than what you might pay for next-day delivery directly with Yamato Transport, which is generally around the 3,000 yen mark. While Yamato is a very reliable service, and arguably the most popular, it still runs largely on a Japan-style system, requiring handwritten Waybills and website navigation that can be daunting for first-timers.

The convenience in using Bounce lies in its multilingual, tourist-focused booking app, which allows you to make the reservation quickly and independently, with minimum fuss. Bounce handles the Waybills and logistics for you so all you have to do is drop your luggage off, giving you more time and energy for the journey.

▼ It also helps to reduce the burden on hotel staff, who can be seen looking harried and stressed out by various luggage-related ordeals below.

With more providers joining the luggage-forwarding scene, hands-free travel looks to be getting even easier in Japan, as companies find better ways to cater to the growing number of tourists who are now opting to stay at private rentals rather than conventional hotels. Now all we need is for this locker-based Shinkansen luggage-forwarding service to expand around Japan, so even more suitcases can enjoy their own journeys on the bullet train without getting in the way of their owners.

title: Why do foreign tourists queue up to eat at Tokyo Little House?
description: Little converted Japanese house has a very big following. With tourism booming in Japan, so too are some of the country’s cafes and restaurants that have become popular on social media. For locals who aren’t tapped into the inbound-tourist algorithm, though, the places that are now attracting queues can be a bit of a mystery, […]
content:
Little converted Japanese house has a very big following.

With tourism booming in Japan, so too are some of the country’s cafes and restaurants that have become popular on social media. For locals who aren’t tapped into the inbound-tourist algorithm, though, the places that are now attracting queues can be a bit of a mystery, and that’s the situation our reporter P.K. Sanjun found himself in recently, when he spotted a long line of foreign tourists in Akasaka outside what, at first glance, looked to be an ordinary cafe.

Curious to find out what was attracting them, P.K. decided to return at a less busy time after work, and when he did, he found that the line outside had disappeared. However, as he approached the store, he could see that it was still busy inside, with foreign tourists making up around half the customers.

From the outside, the cafe has a very retro look, and after running a search for it online, P.K. discovered it was actually a 70-year-old traditional Japanese house that has been renovated into a cafe. Sweetly named “Tokyo Little House”, the cafe also serves as a gallery, with several exhibits exploring the “roots of Tokyo” inside.

The second floor has been converted into a lodging, where one group can stay at a time, making it a stylish cafe-and-accommodation combo. For a local like P.K., though, the cafe itself didn’t seem unique enough to explain its popularity, so when he stepped inside and placed an order, he asked staff about the special appeal of the store.

They told him that overseas visitors make up a significant proportion of the cafe’s customers, and queues of foreign tourists outside are a common sight these days. While the cafe has a very nice ambience to it, one of the really big draws for foreign tourists is said to be the cinnamon toast, which is on the menu at 600 yen (US$4).

P.K. immediately ordered it, with a coffee on the side, and was pleased to find that the toast was crunchy and delicious, with a refined, subtle flavour that made it a good match for the relaxed atmosphere of the cafe.

The coffee and toast were excellent, as were the laid-back vibes and friendly customer service. The customers themselves also appeared chill and relaxed, in a way that made P.K. think they must be travellers who already have a good understanding of Japan and want to explore beyond the country’s more famous big-name chains and tourist spots.

P.K. is happy to say he was impressed with his visit to the cafe, and this isn’t the first time he’s been impressed after following crowds of foreign tourists into a place he’s never been before. It just goes to show that sometimes, foreign tourists can introduce a local to a new spot they might not have heard of, and rather than being a tourist trap it might actually turn out to be a real gem.
